elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement to an affiliate without Vendor consent.
elements.evidence: The consent-free carve-out expressly permits Customer to assign the Agreement “to an affiliate.”

elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement to a successor through a merger without Vendor consent.
elements.evidence: The consent-free carve-out covers assignment to “a successor organization by merger.”

elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement to a successor through an acquisition without Vendor consent.
elements.evidence: The consent-free carve-out covers assignment to “a successor organization by ... acquisition.”

elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement to a successor through a sale of substantially all assets without Vendor consent.
elements.evidence: The consent-free carve-out covers assignment to “a successor organization by ... sale of substantially all assets.”

elements.element: Vendor may not assign the Agreement or its rights without Customer consent.
elements.evidence: IBM may not assign “this Agreement or any of its rights hereunder” without Customer's prior written consent.

elements.element: Customer may not unreasonably withhold consent to a Vendor assignment.
elements.evidence: The IBM-assignment restriction expressly states that Customer's consent may not be unreasonably withheld.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign the Agreement or any right under it to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: The absolute competitor prohibition applies only to assignment of “this Agreement.” Unlike the preceding consent restriction, it does not cover assignment of individual “rights hereunder,” leaving those rights potentially assignable to a competitor with consent.

elements.element: Vendor has no termination right arising from Customer's change of control.
elements.evidence: The rendered operative language grants IBM no termination right upon Customer's change of control.

elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement to a successor without consent.
elements.evidence: Customer may assign to a successor organization through the listed transactions notwithstanding the consent requirement.

elements.element: Customer must provide written notice when assigning the Agreement to a successor.
elements.evidence: No written-notice obligation applies to Customer's successor assignments.

elements.element: Vendor may assign the Agreement to a successor without consent.
elements.evidence: IBM remains subject to Customer's prior written consent for every assignment; there is no successor carve-out.

elements.element: Vendor must provide written notice when assigning the Agreement to a successor.
elements.evidence: No written-notice mechanism for IBM successor assignments is included.

elements.element: Customer's assignments other than successor assignments require Vendor consent.
elements.evidence: Customer may assign to an affiliate without consent even when the affiliate is not a successor.

elements.element: Vendor may not unreasonably withhold consent to Customer's assignments requiring consent.
elements.evidence: The Customer-assignment restriction expressly states that IBM's consent may not be unreasonably withheld.

elements.element: Vendor's assignments other than successor assignments may be made with Customer consent.
elements.evidence: Although Customer consent generally applies, assignment of the Agreement to a Customer competitor is absolutely prohibited and cannot be authorized by consent.

elements.element: Customer may not unreasonably withhold consent to Vendor's assignments requiring consent.
elements.evidence: The IBM-assignment restriction expressly states that Customer's consent may not be unreasonably withheld.

result.reason: The redline substantially implements the preferred position, but the absolute competitor prohibition is narrower than the general IBM-assignment restriction: it prohibits assigning the Agreement to a competitor but does not prohibit assigning individual contractual rights to a competitor. The fallback is also incomplete because it lacks mutual written-notice successor rights, keeps IBM successor assignments subject to consent, and exempts Customer affiliate assignments from the fallback consent regime. The changes otherwise preserve the existing commercial structure, but no complete preferred or fallback level is reached.
